file: 2 Skulls in China_ Early Humans Outside Africa_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Anatomically modern human beings, believed by many scientists to have first evolved in Africa, may have independently evolved in China and other parts of the world, a joint American-Chinese anthropological team has concluded.
That finding, being reported today in the British journal Nature, is based on the sizes and features of two very old skulls excavated from a site in China's Hubei Province.
The scientists, led by Dr. Li Tianyuan of the Hubei Institute of Archeology and Dennis A. Etler, a post-graduate student in anthropology from the University of California at Berkeley, believe the skulls are at least 350,000 years old and may represent a transition between Homo erectus and Homo sapiens. 
They describe the crania, or brain cases, of the two skulls as the most complete ever found in Asia for fossils of such great age.
Other scientists say the age of the skulls has not been determined precisely enough to support the conclusion that their owners actually lived at about the same time Homo sapiens appeared in Africa. 
But one matter on which paleoanthropologists appear to agree is that if the great age of the Chinese skulls can be confirmed, those specimens will be extremely valuable in helping to decipher the history of human evolution.
Â 
More Modern Features
The two skulls and other contemporary fossils were excavated by Dr. Li and a Chinese team in 1989-90. 
Although Chinese authorities have not allowed either the skulls or plaster casts made from them to leave China on loan, Mr. Etler, who speaks Mandarin, was permitted to work with Dr. Li in a collaborative study.
From the structure of rock sediments in which the skulls were embedded and from the remains of other animals in the same sediments, the scientists inferred that the human skulls date from the middle Pleistocene epoch some 350,000 or more years ago. 
More precise dating by measurement of ratios of radioactive isotopes has not been completed, Mr. Etler said in an interview.
Dr. Li and Mr. Etler evaluated 28 characteristics of the skulls, comparing them with comparable characteristics of other fossil human skulls. 
The best preserved of the two Chinese fossils has a long, low cranial vault, parietal bones that converge in a characteristic way, and other features that mark it as belonging to the species Homo erectus, the precursor of Homo sapiens. 
Homo erectus appeared in the fossil record some two million years ago and survived until less than 500,000 years ago.
But Dr. Li and Mr. Etler found other characteristics in the Chinese fossils not typical of Homo erectus but more similar to those of Homo sapiens -- the immediate ancestors of modern man (which is designated Homo sapiens sapiens). 
The more modern features include a rather flat face and sharply angled cheek bones. 
The Chinese skulls thus appear to the two scientists to represent a transitional blend of Homo erectus with Homo sapiens.
Paleoanthropologists are in broad agreement that Homo erectus originated in Africa and later migrated to other parts of the world. 
Among the first fossils scientists discovered of that species (formerly called Pithecanthropus erectus) were those unearthed before World War II in Java and China, and Homo erectus has also been found in Greece and elsewhere in Europe.
But there is little agreement among anthropologists as to where Homo sapiens started out.
"Dr. Li and I believe that alternatives to the idea that Homo sapiens originated in Africa are possible," Mr. Etler said. 
"We believe that modern man may have developed independently in various parts of the world from Homo erectus ancestors, migrating, intermingling, and finally fusing together as a kind of amalgam that we call Homo sapiens. 
Another possibility is that Homo sapiens actually began in China and radiated from there."
Dr. Philip Rightmire of the State University of New York at Binghamton is one of the scientists who sharply disagree.
"This is a controversial subject," he said, "but I do not believe in a multiregional origin for Homo sapiens."
The history of the human genus is one of movement, which for Homo erectus, began from Africa about one million years ago, he said. 
The hypothesis that modern man might have evolved first in Asia is not supported by any evidence, including the fossils studied by Dr. Li and Mr. Etler, he said.
Dr. Rightmire, who has examined photographs of the fossils, believes they are those of early Homo sapiens, not Homo erectus, and that their estimated age of more than 350,000 has yet to be proved. 
The features that Dr. Li and Mr. Etler believe mark the fossils as those of Homo erectus are so badly distorted, Dr. Rightmire said, that no conclusions can be drawn from them.
"Paleoanthropology is always controversial, even when specimens are well preserved, which these skulls are not," he said. 
"Neither the dates of the fossils nor their original shapes, which are squashed and crusted with some of the rock in which they were embedded, are yet known with any accuracy."
Mr. Etler acknowledged that the bones are too distorted to make definitive measurements, but said their general forms are suggestive.
Â 
Role of Ethnic Pride
"Others may disagree with our interpretation, and that's fine," he said. 
"But we felt it was important to bring this great Chinese material to the attention of scholars in the West."
Some scientists, including Dr. Rightmire, suggest that Chinese ethnic pride might color contentions by Chinese scientists that modern human beings might have evolved in China rather than Africa. 
Dr. Etler counters that a similar but opposite bias may color the theorizing of British and American paleoanthropologists who work exclusively with African fossils.
The recent discovery of a 1.6-million-year-old Homo erectus jawbone in the former Soviet republic of Georgia suggests that that species migrated from Africa much earlier than was formerly believed, and that modern man therefore had plenty of time to develop from his primitive ancestors in many parts of the world besides Africa, Mr. Etler said.

file: A History of Asian Ceramics, All in One Place.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN the pottery and porcelain of most of the world, there are few developments that do not have some relation to Chinese ceramics. 
An exhibition that gives some sense of the evolution and highlights of Chinese ceramics, as well as a shorter history of Japanese ceramics, can be seen at the Asia Society in Manhattan through Sept. 
3.
The show covers five major periods of Chinese ceramics: the Tang dynasty (618 to 907), notable for glazed earthenware; the Song dynasty (960 to 1279), known for its stoneware and the green glaze known as celadon; the Yuan dynasty (1279 to 1368), when porcelain began to appear; the Ming dynasty (1368 to 1644), associated with blue and white wares, and the Qing dynasty (1644 to 1912), notable for rich floral porcelains.
The first object the viewer sees is a striking glazed earthenware horse about 30 inches long. 
The realistically modeled cream and tan animal is a tomb figure from the Tang dynasty, dated around the eighth century, as is a glazed sculpture of a court lady playing cymbals. 
She was probably one figure in a funerary set that would have constituted a whole burial orchestra.
Celadon ware from northern China in the Song dynasty is not as familiar as the pale, rich jadelike celadon of southern China. 
The olive-hued glaze on several small northern pieces in the show is incised with stylized leaves and flowers.
Chinese ceramics were traded over much of the world. 
A 17th-century platter showing a gazelle in a garden belonged to Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal.
The exhibition, in which all the work is from the Asia Society's permanent collection, includes a number of Ming pieces in blue and white porcelain. 
On many dragons cavort among waves or clouds. 
The Chinese section ends with a few examples of fruit and flower paintings on porcelain, a technique perfected under the Manchus in the Qing dynasty.
The Japanese work that makes up the rest of the ceramics exhibition covers a shorter but important stretch of time: the 17th and 18th centuries. 
This era saw the development of porcelain in Japan, the expansion of the Japanese export market, the emergence of legendary potters like Ninsei and Kakiemon and the continued creation of pieces for the traditional tea ceremony.
Among the stoneware tea-ceremony objects on display is a modern-looking square dish with a broad ceramic handle used as a food tray. 
There is also a tea storage jar boldly painted with black birds on a cream glaze by Ninsei, a mid-17th-century potter known for his masterful painting on earthenware.
Among the porcelain pieces are several figures. 
Two guardian lions, about 10 inches high, are elaborately patterned and colored in the style of Kakiemon. 
The first potter named Kakiemon, or his son, is credited with establishing overglaze painting on porcelain in the last third of the 17th century.
Also on view at the Asia Society, 725 Park Avenue (70th Street), is a continuing exhibition of Korean porcelain of the Yi dynasty (1392 to 1910). 
Since both Korean and Chinese ceramics influenced Japanese work, it is interesting to compare all three.

file: ANTIQUES_Ancient Chinese Alchemy_ Turning Bronze Into Art.txt
text:
ï»¿
Ancient Chinese bronzes, aglow with brilliant green patinas or polished to mirror brightness, are combined with less pristine vessels encrusted with mud or corrosion in a new exhibition at the China House Gallery, 125 East 65th Street. 
The unorthodox mix of the glorious and the gross can be seen in "Ancient Chinese Bronze Art: Casting the Precious Sacral Vessel," through June 15. 
The exhibition documents how bronzes were made between 2205 and 256 B.C. and how they are restored.
The show's emphasis on metal technology determined the selection of the 41 period bronzes lent by 21 collections in the United States. 
The surface decorations of the vessels range from minimal cord markings to bold mythological images, calligraphic symbols, malachite chips or inlays of copper wire.
To illustrate the casting processes developed in China 4,000 years ago, the Shanghai Museum sent facsimile molds, photographs showing metalworking techniques and reproductions of ancient bronzes. 
From other sources came fragments of original molds, several elaborately restored vessels and two forgeries.
"If you want to understand the evolution of these vessels and why they look the way they do, you have to understand how they are made," said the show's guest curator, W. Thomas Chase, who is head conservator of the Freer Gallery of Art and the Arthur M. Sackler Gallery of the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. 
An owl-shaped wine jug, described until 1982 as a work of the Song Dynasty (A.D. 960 to 1279) in the Shang style, was re-identified when the bronze it is made of was tested and found to be from the Shang Dynasty, which is 2,000 years earlier.
The chronological organization of the show reveals much about the evolution of bronzes. 
The first object, one of the earliest known such vessels, is a roughly crafted, three-legged pitcher, made between the 19th and 16th centuries B.C. The raised lines belting the waist were carved into a ceramic mold before it was filled with molten bronze. 
From the 13th century B.C. came a more gracefully shaped pitcher, its surface enhanced by masks and scrolls, its handsomely curved spout flanked by knobs and its tall tapered legs engagingly raked.
Knowing which comes first -- the vessel or its surface decoration -- may pique the curiosity of some people, but it is not necessary to enjoy these bronzes. 
A case in point is a remarkable narrow-necked flask with copper fretwork on the front and back. 
According to Mr. Chase, tests revealed that the fretwork was placed in the mold first and the vessel was then affixed by casting it to the wafer-thin sheets. 
"If you want to do things just by casting," Mr. Chase said, "this is amazingly elegant solution."
Several objects show varying degrees of corrosion. 
Mr. Chase suggests that the red splotches in the bright green patina of a large jar from the sixth or fifth century B.C. may have developed when acid was used to remove corrosion from the lacelike ribbons banding the surface. 
Whatever the cause, the color from the copper oxide heightens the delicacy of the decoration.
When deterioration is far advanced, it can be less pleasing, as is seen in a wide-mouthed Shang pot made between the 13th and 11th centuries B.C. This vessel is dull gray, and its surface, eaten away by time and the elements, is full of holes. 
In sharp contrast to the elaborate restorations probably made in China before World War II by a skillful artisan, the images on the unrestored half of the pot are fuzzy or totally erased. 
The piece was lent by the Art Museum at Princeton University, a gift from a collector who discovered the modern repairs only after he bought the vessel and had it X-rayed.
An even more audacious fabrication -- at least to Western eyes -- is a trumpet-shaped beaker, 85 percent of which is new. 
The forgery includes only five original fragments that form the base. 
The rest of the beaker, made of brass and lead, may date from the early 20th century.
"The reconstruction, most certainly done in China, shows the extent to which the Chinese will go to restore an ancient bronze," Mr. Chase said.
According to J. May Lee, director of the China House Gallery, the concept of museums is very new in China. 
"Displays are educational, and the Chinese want to show as many types of objects as possible," Ms. Lee said. 
"They use reconstructions and facsimiles side by side with unrestored works in their museums."
The gallery's exhibition was financed by the New York State Council on the Arts, the Asian Cultural Council, the Corning Foundation, Grumman International, the Henry Luce Foundation and the Starr Foundation. 
The paperback catalogue ($28) was written by Mr. Chase with Ms. Lee.
A vessel inlaid with malachite from the fourth century B.C. is among the ancient bronzes on display at the China House Gallery.

file: ANTIQUES_Basins and Bowls From the Palaces Of Imperial China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Sir Percival David's 40-year pursuit of ceramics made from the Tang through Ching dynasties took him to Beijing several times in the 1920's and 30's. 
There he acquired extraordinary 10th- to 18th-century treasures installed for centuries in the palaces of China, some of which are on view in ''Imperial Taste: Chinese Ceramics From the Percival David Collection'' at the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts. 
The show of 56 items remains here through Dec. 
10 and will then travel to the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth and the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston.
Sir Percival, an heir to the Sassoon textile and banking fortune, was born in 1892 in Bombay, where his family's mills were located. 
He studied at Bombay University and London University and settled in England, where he became totally immersed in studying and collecting Chinese art. 
In 1924 he traveled to Beijing to view the Imperial collection, much of which he found stored in boxes. 
At his suggestion, these works were uncrated and exhibited in a building he paid to have restored.
The show was a great success, and on Sir Percival's next visit, in 1927, he was named an adviser to the National Palace Museums. 
He also learned that art from the Imperial collection was up for sale. 
After complex negotiations, he acquired about 40 pieces, and he added to his holdings during several more trips in the 1930's. 
In 1952 he donated his collection, and its home, a 19th-century house on Gordon Square in Bloomsbury, to London University.
The exhibition here was organized by the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, where it opened last July, in collaboration with the Percival David Foundation. 
Money came from the National Endowment for the Arts and the Federal Council on the Arts and Humanities. 
Rosemary Scott, the curator of the Percival David Foundation, assembled the show and produced its splendid catalogue ($22.95). 
From the 1,500 objects in the collection she chose 56 ceramics, 31 of which were potted and painted for, or owned by, the princes of the realm.
''It is a very restricted but representative selection,'' said Elizabeth Jackson, the secretary-librarian of the foundation, in a telephone interview from her London office. 
''The exhibition spans the period of the collection and contains some of its finest pieces.''
Thinly potted Tang and Sung vessels are among the show's more exceptional works, in terms of both their form and their subtle decoration. 
A pale gray vase from the ninth century, incised from top to base with the mouths, scales, gills, fins and flipped tails of two fish that seem locked together like Siamese twins, is a marvel of understatement. 
The stark simplicity of a 10th-century spittoon, its flared cone top set on a ball base, is relieved by its silken gray-green glaze.
Several basins and bowls of the 12th and 13th centuries are surfaced with lacy white-on-white tracings of leaves, flowers and calligraphic images. 
One of the most exquisite objects in the show is a 13th-century narrow-necked pear-shape vase glazed icy blue., The crackles on its surface are evenly spaced like stripes. 
This was Sir Percival's favorite vessel and one of the most admired ceramics in the 1935 exhibition of Chinese art treasures he helped to organize. 
That show, sponsored by London's Royal Academy at Burlington House, included loans from China's Imperial collection.
Notable among the later works now on display are several boldly decorated outsize vessels. 
A 25-inch-tall temple vase of the Yuan Dynasty, dated 1351, is described in the catalogue as one of the most important blue and white porcelains in existence. 
From chrysanthemum scrolls at the top to peonies at the base, the vessel is lavishly decorated. 
Its handles are blue elephant heads, and its body is covered with soaring phoenixes and a dragon that sweeps around the vase enveloped in clouds.
A wilder white dragon decorates a robust blue Ming flask, one of very few vessels ornamented with this reverse decoration. 
A Ming turquoise wine jar the size of a soccer ball is decorated with a gilded copper collar and calligraphy aligned like a zipper below the neck. 
The 18th-century porcelain teapots, jars and dishes are more delicately decorated with birds and blossoms.
''Imperial provenance and Imperial association have become essential parts of the price structure in the market,'' said James J. Lally, a New York dealer in Oriental art. 
''It always was there, but now it has a renewed importance with the advent of Taiwanese and some Hong Kong collectors who share this taste. 
Any porcelain in the market today is worth significantly more if it has an Imperial reign mark.''
Imperial reign marks, designating ceramics made for the sovereigns of China, are scarce, but vessels known to have been in a palace collection and others of comparable refinement are commanding extraordinary prices at auction - especially in Sotheby's sales held over the last year in Hong Kong. 
On May 16, a Sung bowl with Imperial association once used by scholars to wash brushes was sold for $2.82 million, a record at auction for Chinese ceramics. 
The buyer was identified as a Chinese man living in Los Angeles.
Two 18th-century porcelain bowls, decorated with enamels by artisans at the Beijing palace workshops, brought $1 million each in different sales. 
One, a Kang-hsi vessel formerly in Sir Percival's collection that was sold in May, is glazed a bright pink and decorated with a sinuous branch. 
The other, a Chien-lung vessel auctioned a year ago, is painted with pink flowers and landscapes on a yellow ground.

ï»¿
Landscapes, Greek gods or exotic Indian flowers - penned in black on white, white on black or brown on gold - cover virtually every inch of the surfaces of 87 chests, tables, game trays and boxes exhibited at Hyde Park Antiques, 836 Broadway (at 13th Street).
These delightful if excessively decorated objects are exhibited in ''Penwork: the Triumph of Line,'' a show on view through Nov. 
10 that is believed to be the first in New York on this esoteric subject. 
Most of the furnishings date from 1790 to 1830 and were made in England, Scotland, India or China. 
All but two - a Regency daybed in the Greek style with scrolled frame and downswept fluted legs, and a box delicately decorated with charioteers - are for sale.
The most lavishly decorated object in the show is a two-part Regency cabinet, a tour de force of the craft decorated with black ink on a white ground from its cornice to its striped ball feet. 
Dramatizing the doors of the upper cabinet are equestrian studies of Constantine and Charlemagne on rearing horses, heroic figures inspired by the marble statues of Bernini and Cornacchini in St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. 
The inside surfaces - doors, drawer fronts and pigeonholes - come alive with scenes from Homer's ''Iliad,'' inspired by John Flaxman's early-19th-century book illustrations. 
These and other mythological tales are elaborately framed with scrolling leaves and flowers.
''We bought that cabinet in England about a year and a half ago,'' said Bernard Karr, president of Hyde Park. 
''Then we went out looking.''
The search produced 11 more cabinets, 20 tables, 42 boxes, caddies and miniature chests, and 6 handscreens, gaming accessories and the daybed. 
The remainder of the show includes related works embellished with similar images or showing such other craft techniques as transfer printing on plates; an ivory-inlay on an Anglo-Indian table; lacquered decoration on a Chinese tea caddy and an ivory veneer on a miniature Indian bureau bookcase, its surface engravings filled with black lac (shellac).
Penwork - which imitates inlay and veneer in furnishings - proliferated in Britain from the late 18th century through the mid-19th century. 
It was a time when the middle classes developed a taste for the type of picturesque aristocratic furnishings that were fashionable in the great country houses of the period. 
Fanciful furniture covered with meticulously detailed images - especially of the ancient world - was executed in wood veneers, or inlays of marble, wood or metal. 
The subjects depicted were borrowed from every source imaginable - engravings, book illustrations, block-printed textiles and transfer-printed pottery.
The exact roots of the craft are unknown, said Patrick Broome, Hyde Park's director, who organized the exhibition and did the research for its catalogue ($10). 
Proceeds from the sale of the catalogue go to the Historic House Trust, a New York organization that maintains 15 historic houses in the Metropolitan area.
Helping further to document the sources of penwork is the example Mr. Broome found of a richly detailed neoclassical black-and-white 1730's panel, the top of a George II table. 
This panel, an 18th-century example of the ancient Roman technique called scagliola, was created with powdered and colored selenite, a gypsumlike material, applied to a gesso backing. 
The image was dried in high heat and polished.
Penwork, a craft that is far less costly and intricate, became popular 70 years later because it produced similar images if less impressive effects. 
The furniture and box surfaces were first covered with a coat of white lacquer or paint, on which black ink decoration was applied by quill pen. 
Sometimes the technique was reversed, using white ink on a black ground, or it was varied, using brown ink on unpainted wood surfaces that turned golden when shellac was applied. 
Shellac was also used as a finish on black-on-white pieces, darkening some white surfaces to pale yellow.
The most memorable examples are less fussy and more adventurous, using simpler and less predictable images. 
A rare set of trays and cups for the game of Loo, made about 1820, are enlivened with images of playing cards. 
A tea caddy in the shape of a sarcophagus is an amusing study that uses near-caricatures of neoclassical figures. 
Another excellent example is a low two-door Regency cabinet from about 1815, boldly decorated with stylized Indian flowers in white on a black ground that were probably borrowed from a textile. 
Oriental themes show up on other pieces of furniture, including a dome-topped table cabinet from about 1815, its top, doors, and sides decorated in chinoiserie - French-style Chinese figures.
Tables, the least interesting form, dominate as a category in this show, an indication of their popularity 175 years ago. 
Most were made to serve as work tables by day - there are drawers in most of them to store sewing supplies - and gaming tables at night. 
One depicts Saracens and Knights on the squares of its checkerboard-patterned top.
The items in the show range from $480 for a small box to $250,000 for the Regency two-part cabinet. 
The two-door cabinet is $40,000. 
While the finest examples of offbeat penwork furnishings have increased dramatically in price, more modest ones are still occasionally available at prices in the low four figures.
This was seen last weekend in Christie's auction of English furniture in which there were two pieces of penwork furniture. 
A fine Regency sideboard splashed with grotesques, Indian flowers and exotic beasts estimated to bring $30,000 to $40,000, was sold for $121,000 to an American dealer who was not identified. 
A Regency table on paw feet in the neoclassical taste - decorated with gods, goddesses, fruits and leafage, which was expected to sell for $5,000 to $7,000, was bought by Hyde Park for $4,400.
The design of this two-door Regency cabinet (c. 
1815) was probably inspired by an Indian textile.

file: Beijing Journal_China Is Fighting for Its Soul_ Its Looted Antiques.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was not drugs the peasant was selling under the cover of darkness, but something just as restricted, and he was very careful as he displayed his wares on a quiet street before dawn.
"Ming Dynasty," the peasant, a thin man in his 40's, nervously told a dealer, who was crouched down, scrutinizing the blue-and-white porcelain vases. 
If they really did date from the Ming Dynasty, which collapsed in 1644, then they were probably dug from a tomb and are barred from leaving the country.
Smuggling of antiques can be punishable by death in China, but such transactions are nonetheless very common. 
The Government estimates that 40,000 tombs were robbed in 1989 and 1990 alone, and gangs manage to smuggle out huge statues 1,000 years old or more.
Some smugglers show Western collectors photos -- even faxes -- of important pieces in Chinese museums, which often have poor security. 
If they receive an order, the smugglers steal them from the museum and whisk them secretly to a boat waiting somewhere along China's 11,000-mile coastline.
Â 
Joy and Heartache
Encouraged by China's push toward a market economy and by the piles of money they believe Chinese art fetches, smugglers have refined a business that is causing a mixture of joy and heartache on both sides of the Chinese border. 
Art-starved Western collectors -- even some large museums -- have been able to fill their yearning for a neolithic pot or a Song Dynasty ceramic, as Chinese smugglers fill their pockets with money.
But the Government is horrified that national treasures are being stolen. 
Archeologists and historians are also distraught that troves of information are being erased by rampant, careless excavation of tombs.
"A nation's antiquities are a nation's soul," said Kwang-Chih Chang, a professor of Chinese archeology at Harvard University. 
"Antiquities are destroyed every day all over the world by natural disasters, by floods, by construction. 
But when we can control the destruction, it behooves us to do so."
These days, the Government is fighting back harder than ever. 
In the last couple of years it nearly tripled the amount of money spent on protecting its relics. 
This year it coordinated a nationwide crackdown, bringing together museum officials, customs agents, police chiefs and even two Politburo members to publicize the crackdown.
A result is that the smuggling of antiques, especially first-rate ones, seems to have declined. 
In previous years, antiques shops in Hong Kong displayed shelves of glazed pottery, jades, bronzes, clay horse heads and silver objects. 
But now the shops look depleted.
Still, grave robbers and smugglers are clinging to work. 
Late in October in Shaanxi Province in northern China, where Chinese archeologists have discovered the tombs of 72 emperors and 1,240 royal families, a gang of robbers used explosives, searchlights and guns in digging up a tomb from the Tang Dynasty, which reigned from the seventh to 10th centuries.
This year thousands of villagers openly plundered a group of tombs in Shaanxi, Chinese press reports say. 
Tomb robbery has been especially severe in the provinces of Shaanxi, Henan, Gansu and Jiangsu, as well as in the city of Shanghai.
Museum robberies are also a problem, in part because the museums cannot afford adequate security systems. 
About four years ago, when Sotheby's was planning to auction an ancient bronze vessel, perhaps 3,000 years old, an art expert who had read the catalogue wrote to the Chinese authorities asking them to check whether the piece had been smuggled from China.
Â 
Beauty Comes First
The authorities discovered that the vessel had been stolen from a small county museum in Hubei Province and they had the photographs and documents to prove it. 
The owner returned the vessel to China, and the Chinese thief was caught and sentenced to death.
Local Chinese authorities are often much less concerned with preserving their culture than the central Government. 
Some prefer to have money instead of what they regard as old pieces of pottery that only clutter up warehouses.
James J. Lally, a Chinese art dealer based in New York, explained how a businessman was able to take six 16th-century Ming Dynasty stone sculptures out of China. 
What was remarkable was that these sculptures -- horses, rams and tigers -- were all life size.
Local officials evidently let him take the carvings across the border because they regarded them as little more than a pile of stones that farmers kept bumping into when they planted.
But the appetite for rare antiques means that the vigorous debate about how they reach the West is likely to persist among lovers of art. 
Archeologists are often outraged by the smuggling while dealers and collectors say that bronzes and statues that get out of China are often better preserved than those that remain, and that such pieces help arouse public awareness of Asian art.
"The way the art market regards works of art is first and foremost for their beauty," Mr. Lally said. 
"The hierarchy of what's important to know is sometimes the reverse for an art lover than it is for an archeologist."

file: CAMPUS LIFE_ Berkeley_Scholars in China Discover a Meal By Early Man.txt
text:
ï»¿
Finding human teeth marks on a million-year-old elephant ankle made waiting a lifetime to dig in China worthwhile for an anthropology professor at the University of California at Berkeley.
A team of American and Chinese anthropologists led by Emeritus Prof. Desmond Clark -- who in 1981 in Ethopia was a co-discoverer of some of the oldest human remains found to date -- recently received the first grant for non-Chinese to conduct excavations in China since before World War II.
Professor Clark said team members in China are examining a pile of old broken bones and stones that were discovered this summer in the Nihewan Basin, northwest of Beijing, hoping to find clues of how early hominids lived.
"It was difficult during the Cultural Revolution for foreigners to research in China," Professor Clark said. 
"We could look at the site with our Chinese colleagues but could not participate in excavations. 
This is truly exciting and has finally happened."
Â 
A Find After Days of Sifting
The Chinese-American team began excavations and surveys in July, a month after its permit was issued.
After four days of sifting through fine-grained sands, a team member uncovered an ankle bone belonging to an elephant dating from more than a million years ago, said Dennis Etler, a Berkeley anthropology graduate student from Lakewood, N.J.
Human teeth and cut marks on the bone indicated that humans, not large mammals like as hyenas, had been gnawing on the bones, Professor Clark said.
The cut marks could have been caused by sharp-edged rocks or flakes, many of which were found alongside the bones, Mr. Etler said. 
"These flakes were possibly used as tools to scrape loose the meat," he said.
But finding beautifully fashioned tools or the remains of early humans -- million-year-old hominid fossils have already been discovered -- is not what the team is after. 
"We not only want to establish early presence of homo erectus, but we want to figure out how they behaved," said Kathy Schick, an archeology professor at the University of Indiana at Bloomington who is on the China team.
Â 
Techniques New to Chinese
In addition to the excavations, Frank Brown, a team member and geology professor at the University of Utah, taught seminars for Chinese scientists.
Modern excavation and survey techniques introduced by the American scientists were new to the Chinese scientists, Professor Clark said. 
"Because the Chinese Government forbade foreigners from excavating, the Chinese were not exposed to these modern techniques now used internationally by archeologists."
Professor Clark's Chinese counterpart on the team, Jui Lanpo, pressured the Government to ease its restrictions, Mr. Etler said. 
(Mr. Lanpo was working on the excavation site when the 450,000-year-old remains of Peking Man, the first hominid remains found in China, were unearthed in the 1920's.)
Lifting the ban, however, has reciprocal advantages, Professor Clark said in a recent interview. 
Until now, foreigners have not had the opportunity to dig in undisturbed sites like the Nihewan Basin.
Â 
Educating Chinese Scientists
As part of the effort to educate the younger Chinese scientists in the group, Professor Schick arranged for two of them to work this semester at the University of Indiana as research scholars. 
In June 1992 Professor Clark is scheduled to teach for a semester at Beijing University.
The $60,000-a-year a year project, financed by the Henry Luce Foundation in New York, will resume in April and continue over the next three summers.
The 15 team members include scientists from the Chinese Academy's Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing and Nicholas Toth, an anthropology professor at the University of Indiana at Bloomington.

SEAL CARVINGS
The small square markings, or seals, that one sees in the corners of Chinese works of art are the subject of an exhibition at the Yale Art Gallery. 
Conceived by Qianshen Bai, a graduate student in the history of art and a practitioner of the art of seal carving, the exhibition highlights an obscure but important element of Chinese culture.
"The World Within a Square Inch," which will remain on view through July 31, consists of 50 handscrolls, hanging scrolls, album leaves, tile rubbings, bronze and porcelain objects, a set of seal carver's tools and magnified impressions of seals that permit the viewer to appreciate their intricacy.
The seals are carved on stones selected for their color, texture and markings in a tradition of inscription that dates to 1400 B.C. The examples on view, mostly from the 19th and 20th centuries, were donated by seal carvers from China andby private collectors.
Widely regarded as antique stamps of ownership and links to China's long history, seals are gaining acceptance as a contemporary art form by young carvers who are developing innovative techniques. 
A lecture, "Seals and Seal Carving in Chinese Culture: From Symbol of Office to Scholarly Art Form," will be delivered by Colin C. Mackenzie, associate curator of Asian art, on Tuesday at 2 P.M. and again on Thursday at 1 P.M. Admission is free.

ROCKY HORROR SHOW
The "Rocky Horror Show," an audience participation show that was first presented at the Royal Court Theater in London in 1973, continues to be performed in London as well as in the United States. 
Its latest venue is the Downtown Cabaret Theater in Bridgeport, where it may be seen live through Aug. 
8; the show should not be confused with "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," a cinematic version usually shown at midnight, in deference to the Frankenstein legend on which the scenario is based.
The cabaret has suspended its bring-your-own-refreshments policy for the duration of the run, and advises patrons that children should be left at home. 
For that matter so should adults who might be offended by some of the scenes and language, which might be described as lunatic or raunchy. 
But for most audiences "Rocky Horror" is just good fun.
Performance times this week are Friday at 7:30 and 10 P.M. and Saturday at 7 and 10 P.M. Starting June 5, performances are scheduled on Thursday, Friday and Saturday at 10 P.M. only.

QUILTS FROM 1840
More than 30 quilts dating to 1840 will be on display at the East Haddam Historical Museum on the Moodus Green beginning tomorrow from 9 A.M. to 1 P.M. and continuing through June 21 on Wednesdays through Sundays from 1 to 5 P.M.
Fifteen quilts have been hung, the rest are folded on tables, too fragile to hang. 
The patterns include Irish Chain, Flower Basket, Feathered Star, Double Wedding Ring, Victorian Crazy Quilt, Flower Garden, Log Cabin, Mosaic and Shoo-Fly. 
All were created by women who lived in the area up to about 1910; the quilts have been kept in excellent condition, and lent to the museum for this exhibition.

KALEIDOSCOPE IMAGES
"Kaleido Sight" is the first of several permanent exhibitions to be completed before the opening of a 130,000-square-foot Science Museum of Connecticut in 1995. 
The exhibits will be shown to the public in the existing building at 950 Trout Brook Drive in West Hartford, then moved to the new complex in East Hartford.
The Kaleido Sight is a 30-foot computerized kaleidoscope that delivers some startling images. 
The viewer stands at the front, where the eye would be on a hand-held kaleidoscope, then picks up a wand and waves it. 
The wand, hand, face, and movements are picked up by a camera that sends the pictures to the computer, which in turn adds color and motion. 
Dual mirrors then create symmetrical hexagonal images, increasing dramatically in size as the viewer walks toward the center of the tunnel.
In 1985 the museum changed its name from the Children's Museum of Hartford, and began to expand into a complex that would be of interest to adults as well as children. 
The museum, which received part of a $13 million grant to Connecticut by the National Science Foundation, has embarked on the building program at a two-acre site on the Connecticut River, at the end of East River Drive. 
An additional seven acres of adjacent wetlands will be at the disposal of the museum for environmental programs.
A committee of advisors from Yale and Wesleyan Universities, United Technologies and other science-oriented companies are working on ideas for exhibition themes based on robotics, biotechnology, computer applications, energy systems, the Connecticut River environment and other elements important to the state's future.

POSTER ART
Posters are a relatively new form of expression, beginning in the 19th century and elevated to high art by Toulouse-Lautrec and other painters of the period. 
Political posters were introduced later, in the early part of this century, generated by World War I and the Russian Revolution.
An exhibition of more than 500 German and Russian posters from around 1915 to 1925, priced from $40 to $3,000 depending on their rarity, is on display in Ridgefield through June 13 at the Antique Poster Collection, 17 Danbury Road.
Perceived as early examples of the use of art as propaganda, political posters have become collector's items. 
Executed as caricature, realistically or heroically, they were calculated to command attention. 
The artists who created them considered the task to be a duty to the state, whether to garner support for a political party, increase productivity, or crush the enemy.
The gallery is open Tuesday through Saturday from 10 A.M. to 4 P.M. More information: 438-1836.

EMBROIDERED serpents with long fangs prance and grimace on 19th-century silk robes from China in a dazzling exhibition, "Dragon Threads," at the Newark Museum.
The five-clawed dragon was designated as the official emblem of the emperor in 206 B.C. Through the centuries, this sign has been emblazoned on everything that belonged to the emperor and his immediate family. 
The Chinese regime became known as the Dragon Throne.
Although dragon robes were de rigueur for all court functions, only the imperial family could wear clothing with five-clawed dragons. 
During the last era of empire, the Ching Dynasty (1644-1912), the colors of the royal family's silks also signified their high rank: lemon yellow was reserved for the emperor, apricot yellow for the first-born prince and and golden yellow for the other sons.
One princely robe, in an apricot hue, is stitched with eight golden dragons, which twist and snarl across the front, back and sleeves. 
Other "auspicious symbols" include billowing waves and rocks along the lower border, to signify the earth and seas, while wispy blue and green clouds, bright blossoms and flames float across the heavens.
Iris Barrel Apfel, who collected the textiles in this exhibition, said that "this symbolism is only complete when the coat is worn" and that "the human body becomes the world axis and the neck opening, the gate of heaven."
At the time of marriage, even a village bride could become an "empress for a day" by wearing clothing emblazoned with a four-clawed imperial dragon. 
Brides represented yin, the female force that must combine with the masculine yang to insure human survival.
In this show, a wedding jacket is decorated with butterflies, the Chinese equivalent of Cupid. 
And these brides wore red, the color of virtue, joy and festivities.
During her engagement, a young women was secluded in her family home. 
What did she do?
Embroider, of course. 
A trousseau usually consisted of elaborate collars, 12 to 100 pairs of decorated shoes, and the cover and canopy for the bridal bed. 
Guests at the wedding felt free to critique a display of the bride's skill with needle and thread, Mrs. Apfel said.
After marriage, the embroidery tasks continued. 
Wives were expected to decorate their own wardrobes, wall hangings, tablecloths, canopies and covers for beds, the altar and mirrors.
If sons were born, their garments were usually bright and trimmed with grimacing creatures. 
The two tiger-head hats with fangs and flowery ears would entice even today's Ninja Turtle devotees. 
But a young girl's robe, trimmed with bunches of grapes and butterflies, is more refined. 
Her playtime activities must have been restricted, since this embroidered and appliqued silk dress is in perfect condition.
Antique textiles are fragile, so these sumptuous robes are rarely exhibited. 
"They need time to rest," Mrs. Apfel said.
Approximately one-third of the more than 100 robes and accessories on display have been donated to the Newark Museum's Asian Collections by Mrs. Apfel and her Attata Foundation (an acronym created from the words "antique textiles" in English, French and Italian).
Mrs. Apfel's search for these fabric treasures, which began in 1953, led her "into noisy street markets, dank cellars, dusty attics and into expensive auction rooms and elegant antique shops," she said.
A stylized version of a crimson Chinese garden pavilion with a royal yellow roof and short picket fence dominates the gallery. 
The atmosphere is of another place, another time, without the artifice of a re-created period room. 
Flat, headless figures display the robes with outstretched arms so that details are not hidden among the folds.
And these details are intriguing. 
The side closing, which always buttons under the right arm, is usually edged with a decorative border or two, replete with flowers or animals. 
Cuffs echo the symbolic motifs and colors of a robe. 
One processional robe is dotted with the "shou" character, meaning long life.
A patient and careful inspection can enrich the viewer's enjoyment of this exhibition. 
One woman's jacket features miniature scenes, no more than an inch and a half in any direction. 
Each one depicts a garden with one or two women holding a lute or potted plant. 
Others show courtiers crossing arched bridges. 
The perfection and charm of this minute workmanship is spellbinding.
Mrs. Apfel said that ancient Ching archives estimated the time required to complete a single robe. 
Drawing the designs took two weeks; 13 months were spent stitching the gold threads; another year passed before the embroidery was finished.
The legendary long fingernails of Chinese women did not interfere with their fine needlework. 
"They only had one or two long nails, and those were not on both hands," she said.
But another legendary account is true: about the age of 6, little girls did have their foot bones broken and bandaged. 
This torturous process produced grown women with "lotus bud" feet, which gave them social status. 
Although the practice was outlawed, it continued until the end of the Ching Dynasty. 
Some of the decorated shoes on display are barely four and a half inches long.
A group of jewelry, hair ornaments and a headdress all gleam in a heavenly shade of iridescent blue. 
The source of this exotic hue: feathers of the tiny kingfisher bird, which were cut to shape and set in gold and silver with semiprecious jewels. 
As with the egret, the popularity of the plumage of this bird nearly caused its extinction.
Displays of hand and stick puppets portray the nobility in their full regalia, plus some sweet-faced or evil-looking characters who must have added drama to the plots. 
Mrs. Apfel said that Ching puppeteers carved, painted and embroidered the clothing of their puppets and then performed all the parts. 
These artistic traditions and puppets were passed down from father to son.
A small side exhibition explains sericulture, the silk industry. 
Millions of Chinese were once employed in the raising and feeding of silkworms and the reeling and weaving of their precious filaments. 
There are cocoons, wound with the long delicate threads, and a skein of white silk strands.
There will be a Chinese Festival in the Junior Museum on Dec. 
30 from 1 to 4 P.M. "Claws and Panther Paws," for ages 3 to 15, will include hands-on workshops, noodle-pulling demonstrations and performances by the Asian American Dance Theater.
"Dragon Threads" will continue through Jan. 
3. The Newark Museum, at 49 Washington Street, is open from noon to 5 P.M. Wednesday through Sunday, but closed on Christmas and New Year's Day. 
Admission is free.

text:
ï»¿
EARLY in the movie ''Gorillas in the Mist,'' Sigourney Weaver, as the naturalist Dian Fossey, flees headlong down a mountain slope, pursued by a roaring male gorilla. 
''What does Schaller's book say when a gorilla charges?'' her tracker asks moments later as she recovers in safety.
''It says, 'Never run,' '' replies Ms. Fossey, who studied and fiercely protected Africa's mountain gorillas before she was murdered in 1985.
The offscreen, real-life author of the book is George B. Schaller, the science director of Wildlife Conservation International, the global conservation arm of the New York Zoological Society. 
He is perhaps the most famous field biologist in the world today, and over the last three decades he has stood up to more than his share of challenges in the wild.
In the interest of science and conservation, he has confronted lions in the Serengeti Plain in Africa, tigers in India and snow leopards in China. 
He has studied the giant panda up close and worked hard to prevent its disappearance. 
His pioneering study of the mountain gorilla was the first to discover that the species was in danger of extinction, thereby setting the stage for Ms. Fossey's long crusade to save it.
Â 
'Century of Destruction'
But most of all, he has struggled to help reverse the course of what he calls a global ''century of destruction'' in which he believes that humans are destroying natural resources, particularly plants and animals, at such a rate that humans' existence will ultimately be threatened. 
He says he has devoted much of his life to trying to hold the line so that the next century might be one of rehabilitation.
Now, at 56 years old, he is grappling with the biggest single conservation challenge of his life: the effort to understand and preserve what he calls ''the last really large, unspoiled ecosystem'' on earth aside from parts of the polar ice caps and some mountaintops.
It is the Qian Tang region of northwest Tibet, a vast, bleak territory of sparsely grassed plains broken by hills, valleys, lakes and snowy peaks, populated by wild yaks and asses, lyre-horned Tibetan antelopes, gazelles, blue sheep and, in the higher elevations, snow leopards. 
Some of the animals are found nowhere else on earth.
Dr. Schaller, who is the only Western biologist working in the region, disclosed last week in New York that he and Chinese officials had agreed to create in the Qian Tang what they say will be the world's largest wildlife reserve. 
It would be about the size of Colorado and cover about one-fifth of Tibet's area. 
Qian Tang (pronounced chahng tahng), meaning ''northern plain,'' is largely unexplored, mostly undisturbed and all but uninhabited. 
Only a few herdsmen enter it at certain seasons to hunt for meat and hides. 
The herdsmen will still be allowed to do so under the letter of intent signed by Dr. Schaller and Chinese officials last Nov. 
29 in Lhasa, the Tibetan capital. 
But all other hunting will be prohibited, and the Chinese Government will manage the reserve as a protected area, with both expert help and material aid from Wildlife Conservation International.
Â 
Fear of Lost Opportunity
As with the American Plains a century or two ago, development is already lapping at the edges of the planned reserve. 
If the worldwide urge ''to develop the last bit of land for human use'' is given free play there, Dr. Schaller said, hunting, mining and other commercial activities will despoil the region and a ''unique opportunity'' will slip away.
In pursuit of that opportunity, he has made four expeditions to the Qian Tang along with Chinese and Tibetan colleagues over the last decade. 
He is planning to make a fifth this summer in a massive effort to delineate and define the ecosystem and its inhabitants, an essential first step in any conservation program. 
The Chinese Government appears serious about preserving the Qian Tang and if the effort succeeds, he said, it will demonstrate a commitment by China to ''the rational use of its resources.''
It would also be a dramatic demonstration of Dr. Schaller's belief that governments around the globe are at last starting to recognize seriously that the destruction of ecosystems, with all the resources they contain, cannot go on. 
''The world as a whole is beginning to wake up to the realities,'' he said.
Dr. Schaller comes honestly to a global perspective. 
Born in 1933, the son of a German diplomat in Berlin, he lived in a number of European capitals as a child. 
He came to the United States with his mother in 1947.
''My mother did not want to remain in Europe after the war, so she brought my brother and myself,'' he said. 
''My father stayed in Germany.''
Â 
Earning a Living From Hobby
''I've never been interested in anything but the outdoors,'' he said, ''but it wasn't until I got to the university that I discovered you could make a living out of your hobby.''
That was the University of Alaska, where he enrolled after a youthful trip down the Yukon with his cousin. 
He holds two bachelor's degrees from there and a Ph.D. from the University of Wisconsin.
''Alaska remains my spiritual home,'' he said. 
In one of his first major field activities, he took part in the biological survey that preceded the establishment of the vast Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. 
In succeeding years, Dr. Schaller did his work on the ecology and behavior of the mountain gorilla of Africa, the tiger and deer of central India, the lion, wild dog, cheetah and leopard of the Serengeti, the wild sheep and goats of the Himalayas, the jaguar, caiman and marsh deer of Brazil, and the panda and snow leopard of China. 
Along the way, drawing directly on his first-hand research, he has written 11 books and scores of articles.
The Qian Tang, he says, ''has world importance'' and helping to preserve it would be extremely satisfying. 
''You spend years in alien cultures,'' he said, ''often away from from family, from friends, often among people who don't understand you, either your language or what you're really after.''
Traveling by car, carrying their own gasoline, or by horseback or camel or yak or on foot, Dr. Schaller and his Chinese and Tibetan colleagues have so far been able to make spot checks of the Qian Tang's animal populations. 
Now, he said, they are about to engage in hard, detailed surveys of those populations and of the animals' migration ranges.
This sort of detailed work is necessary, he said, if one is to avoid the mistake that has been made at other large preserves like the Serengeti National Park in Tanzania. 
Migratory animals define the limits of such large ecosystems, he explained. 
In the Serengeti, that defining animal is the wildebeest, but the Serengeti park's boundaries were established before it was clear where the wildebeest moved. 
As a result, he said, the wildebeest ranges beyond the park, into agricultural areas hostile to it.
The Qian Tang offers a matchless opportunity to bring a huge, intact ecosystem under protection, he said. 
The vastness of the reserve should encompass its animals' migrations, he said. 
High Point of Career?
Is the Qian Tang venture the capstone of a career?
''The future tends to be hard to predict,'' Dr. Schaller said. 
''If the Chinese are interested and continue their cooperation, I'm certainly most happy to work with the Lhasa and Beijing governments to continue the work.''
While the political upheavals in China and Tibet have made it more difficult to operate there, he said, such difficulties are ''par for any field biologist.''
''When any country has internal problems, you wait it out and then continue, because your concern is long-term conservation,'' he said. 
''Short-term upheavals are really irrelevant to your goals. 
''Conservation transcends politics completely.''

text:
ï»¿
Wang Yani is a prodigy. 
She is largely self-taught. 
She paints rapidly in brush and ink. 
The earliest of the 69 paintings in ''Yani: The Brush of Innocence,'' at the Arthur M. Sackler Gallery, were made when she was 3 and 4 years old. 
She has spent her 14 years in the village of Gongcheng in Guangxi province in southern China, 50 miles from Guilin, which the catalogue says has been renowned since Ming times for ''the most beautiful mountains and waters under heaven.''
There is plenty of exuberance and delight in this problematical and even troubling show. 
The monkeys with which Yani was preoccupied between the ages of 3 and 6 are tireless in their willingness to perform for one another and for her. 
Her large, irked lion - painted when she was 8 - with monkeys pulling his tail and climbing over him like a party of kids on a sleeping father's back, opens one beady eye, turns down his red mouth, and bears them.
Almost everything in these episodic paintings is in a state of expectancy or resolution. 
A monkey with a fishing line has just hooked a fish. 
Trees not only flower but actually offer fruit. 
Wide-eyed birds seem to be waiting for orders to fly. 
Almost every animal is self-confident and proud. 
Only in the children - there are no explicit images of adults, although they are omnipresent in the mountains and trees - is there doubt that happiness is near.
Yani seems to have Chinese painting in her blood. 
Her feeling for every single thing she paints reflects the pantheism that runs like a river through Chinese art. 
Mountains and monkeys, as well as cranes and lotuses, are staples of Chinese painting. 
From the age of 3, Yani has had an awareness of solid and void and of the expressive possibilities of brush and ink. 
She is completely at home on paper.
The exhibition provides a great deal of information. 
According to Jan Stuart, the specialist in Chinese art at the Sackler, who installed the show, there is now in China a particular interest in prodigies. 
Artistic prodigies who are girls are no longer that surprising. 
Nor is the enthusiasm with which Yani has been greeted by a Chinese art establishment largely run by men.
What arouses that enthusiasm is the freshness and youthfulness of her paintings. 
After a period of artistic dogma and oppression, they seem to offer an assurance that new beginnings are possible and that childhood can have the irresistible force of a condition.
In her catalogue essay on ''Wang Yani and Contemporary Chinese Painting,'' the art historian Julia Andrews points out that Mao Zedong died in 1976, when Yani was 1, and suggests that Yani has given the Chinese an image of themselves they need. 
''Her emergence coincided with the severe disillusionment of many older artists in socialist realist art and with a desire to promote experimentation and exploration of other forms. 
The paintings of a child who knew nothing of politics offered a fresh vision that many artists sought in their own work.''
One of the pressures Yani has to live with, however, is that there is now an investment in her ''innocence.''
She is already something of a sideshow. 
''She is a national treasure, and people come from great distances to watch her at work,'' write Lynn T. Goldsmith and David Henry Feldman, developmental psychologists, in the catalogue. 
When the exhibition opened, Yani was in Washington to answer questions and demonstrate her freewheeling techniques.
Wang Shiqiang, Yani's father, formerly a narrative oil painter working in Western styles, wants to protect her from self-consciousness. 
Her feeling for painting has a great deal to do with him. 
When she was tiny, they roamed rivers and fields and visited the zoo where she first encountered the monkeys that made her howl and jump with glee. 
He bought her a pet monkey when she was 3. 
Ms. Stuart said that Yani considers her monkey her best friend.
It was on a trip with her father when she was 2 1/2 that Yani first painted. 
From the beginning, her images and methods were purely Chinese. 
In 1983, when Yani was 8, her father gave up painting. 
He works as a cultural-affairs officer. 
When Yani travels, he accompanies her. 
He keeps a diary of their travels. 
He will decide when she is ready for art books. 
He has kept almost all her paintings, which now number around 10,000. 
None has been sold.
All the family references in the catalogue are to Yani and Shiqiang. 
There is only passing mention of her mother, Tang Fongjiao, even though her presence can be felt throughout Yani's stories. 
She works in a department store. 
It is said that the money she earns buys Yani's art supplies.
There is no indication in the catalogue that Yani even has a brother. 
She does: Wang Qiangyu is 9 years old, and he, too, is exceptionally gifted as a painter. 
The family is considering discouraging him from painting. 
The fear is that his artistic development may inhibit Yani's spontaneity.
In short, this show of paintings made between the ages of 3 and 12 by a wonderfully gifted child needs to be approached with caution. 
There are many possible agendas in it. 
For example, the exhibition was organized by the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City, Mo., with the sponsorship of the Ministry of Culture of the People's Republic of China. 
This museum has been a force in Chinese art, and an exhibition on a contemporary Chinese artist unknown in the United States will help it remain one.
It is significant that a prodigy in a distant, semi-autonomous region of China can be seen in Japan, Europe and the United States when still a prodigy. 
This exhibition is a statement of the will that existed in China to make the world aware of at least some of its cultural energy. 
And it is a statement of the will of the international art world to penetrate every corner of the globe and show art when it is still fresh and hot.
Should this exhibition be taking place?
A number of Yani's paintings are astonishingly finished for a child, but they are not the paintings of an accomplished artist. 
In addition, they are weighed down by the museum setting and by their black frames. 
The best way to see the paintings is in the catalogue, where the rapid succession of images reflects the quickness and concentration with which they were made. 
What this show is, above all, is a fabulous children's book - imagined and painted by a child.
Yani is not ready for the art-historical treatment. 
When Ms. Goldsmith and Mr. Feldman write of the ''significant shift when she is about 6 or 7,'' a ''period'' that can be ''characterized by explorations of a broader range of technical and thematic issues,'' it is absurd.
So is the mythology of production. 
In a generally sensitive catalogue essay, Dr. Wai-ching Ho, a developmental psychologist and the project director for the show, writes that ''by the age of 6 Yani had produced 4,000 paintings'' - a statement proudly repeated in the press release. 
All this does is put pressure on Yani to produce, and turn her into a production machine.
Why is Yani a prodigy?
For one thing, she seems to have been born with an understanding of space and form. 
For another, she not only has the ability to fantasize, but her fantasies are totally accessible to her, and she has absolute faith in their goodness and worth.
The paintings in this show are functional. 
That is to say, what Yani painted was real to her, with real effects. 
In his essay, Dr. Ho relates, ''One day her father bought her a lovely red umbrella. 
Too impatient to wait for the rain to come, she painted a monkey holding a little red umbrella and playing happily in the rain.''
Ms. Goldsmith and Mr. Feldman write that in her paintings Yani ''fed'' her ink monkeys. 
''Sometimes her father would even hear her chiding the painted images to behave, because she was about to share (that is, paint) their fruit.''
These are the works of someone with supreme confidence in herself, in her subject matter and in painting, and who has the ability to make others believe in her magical powers. 
When a painting works, everything in it is personified. 
The smudges and blots of her cliffs and peaks loom like people and animals amid strange and not always friendly activities and games.
From the beginning, Yani has had a remarkable ability to digest psychologically loaded information. 
For example, when she was 4, she painted three images of intoxication. 
In ''Drunk,'' two furry monkeys with red faces are sprawled out on the floor alongside a phallic- and dragon-shaped wine pot made by her father. 
In ''Sniffing the Wine,'' a solitary monkey and the pot seem almost to be kissing each other while loquat fruit shaped like disembodied breast-eyes lie on the floor to one side. 
These images are already sexual and self-conscious. 
They are not innocent. 
Yani is clearly extremely observant, so it is not surprising that the strength of her paintings depends so much upon eyes. 
The most conspicuous aspect of her children are their big eyes. 
The eyes anchor her horses and egrets in space and make them human. 
Even the lotuses she loves so much look as if they can see. 
It is only the larger and more threatening forces, like mountains, that are deprived of sight.
What will happen to Yani?
Certainly she has tremendous resources. 
. Such an artistic prodigy may be conceivable now only far from a big city, in a secure world rooted in tradition. 
Yani still lives in Gongcheng, near mountains and rivers she continues to wander, and to which she feels she belongs. 
She clearly has remarkable intelligence, shrewdness and wit. 
She will need them. 
(After closing at the Arthur M. Sackler Gallery on Oct. 
22, the exhibition will travel to the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City [Dec. 
16 to Jan. 
28] and then to the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco [March 7 to April 29]. 
Financing was provided by United Technologies Corporation.)
