China and the Getty Conservation Institute today announced a joint effort to preserve two of China's largest and most significant cultural sites, where statues and paintings dating from the fourth century are decaying from harsh weather, pollution and damage by earthquakes.
The sites are the Mogao Grottoes on the edge of the Gobi in northwestern China and the Yungang Grottoes, 200 miles west of Beijing. 
Together, the sites contain 545 cave-like temples carved into cliffs. 
The temples contain more than 53,000 clay figures of Buddha, ranging from miniature bas-reliefs to a statue 108 feet high. 
The temples, popular among both Chinese and foreign tourists, also have 484,200 square feet of wall paintings.
The cost of the project has not been determined, but it will be shared by China, the Getty Conservation Institute and Unesco. 
The work is to involve at least 25 preservation specialists from the United States. 
The focus will be on arresting decay, not restoring art already damaged, said Luis Monreal, the director of the Getty Conservation Institute, a private foundation. 
He said the first step would be ''diagnosis'' of the sites and would take 18 months.
Â 
How It Happened
The announcement of the conservation project was made in Los Angeles by Ma Yuzhen, China's Consul General, and Harold M. Williams, the president of the J. Paul Getty Trust, a private foundation. 
The Getty Conservation Institute, a subsidiary of the trust, was created in 1982 and has collaborated with Egypt to preserve the tomb of Queen Nefertari and the royal mummies in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
The possibility of cooperation between China and the Getty was first raised in 1986 by China's National Administrative Bureau for Museums and Archeological Data. 
Last May, Getty representatives visited the sites.
Mr. Yuzhen said the sites contain ''evidence of the astonishing creativity of the ancient Chinese people.''
''The Mogao and Yungang Grottoes are the most magnificent storehouses of Buddhist art in the world,'' he said. 
''Both are national treasures of China.''
''We can provide resources of rescue technology not available now in China,'' Mr. Monreal said. 
''At the same time, field projects of this magnitude provide the international conservation community with valuable information on the application of new materials and technologies.''
Â 
What the Sites Contain
The Mogao Grottoes are near the town of Dunhuang on the edge of the Gobi, 1,100 miles west of Beijing. 
The site includes 492 rock temples with thousands of square feet of wall paintings and 2,000 painted clay figures of Buddha.
Hot summers and frigid winters and sand blown by fierce winds have eroded many of the statues and paintings, peeled off paint and washed out colors. 
Algae and fungus are also problems. 
The area also has frequent earthquakes of medium intensity.
Because of the damage and fears for safety, some of the temple caves are closed to the public, Chinese officials said. 
Although remote, the Mogao Grottoes are accessible by a new airport.
The Yungang Grottoes, near Datong, a coal mining city in northern China, face decay from pollution, salt deposits and the weather. 
There, 53 rock temples are carved into the face of a 1,000-yard-long sandstone cliff.
The Yungang temples contain 51,000 representations of Buddha, ranging from miniature bas-reliefs to statues 60-feet high, all carved directly in the rock. 
Most of the carvings, which date to the year 460, were restored in the Ming Dynasty from 1368-1644. 
The eroded carvings were covered with plaster, which was then redecorated.

ï»¿
Poet in Full Rig
While Jean Cocteau thought of himself as a writer, his real talent was social gesture, in which he successfully combined outrageousness and a passion for French pop. 
Here is his induction into the French Academy, from ''Confessions of a Literary Archaeologist'' by Carlton Lake (New Directions).
At that moment a drummer began a deafening roll, the guards drew their sabres, and through the rear entrance filed the not-quite-forty immortals. 
Most of them were wearing dark business suits, but when Cocteau passed by, I saw that he was resplendent in his full Academy regalia: the embroidered green uniform (not actually green but midnight blue, with green facing), cape, cocked hat (all by Lanvin), and sword. 
Cocteau's sword was not the usual academician's sword. 
Executed by Cartier, its hilt bore various symbols relating to Cocteau's life and work. 
I was unable to make out all of them as he passed, but I could see the hand guard, at least - a profile of Oedipus - and, at the top, the ivory lyre, symbol of the poet.
His Bed Too Was a Canvas
Vincent van Gogh could find homely appeal in almost anything - in this case a streetwalker. 
He's quoted in ''Van Gogh: His Life and His Art'' by David Sweetman (Crown).
I hadn't far to look. 
I found a woman, not young, not beautiful, nothing remarkable, if you like, but perhaps you are somewhat curious. 
She was rather tall and strongly built; she did not have a lady's hands like Kee, but the hands of one who works much; but she was not coarse or common, and had nothing very womanly about her. 
She reminded me of some figure by Chardin or Frere, or perhaps Jan Steen. 
Well, what the French call une ouvriere. 
She had had many cares, one could see that, and life had been hard for her, oh, she was not distinguished, nothing extraordinary, nothing unusual. 
. . . Did we spend much money together?
No, for I did not have much, and I said to her, Listen you and I don't need to make ourselves drunk to feel something for each other; just put what I can spare in your pocket.
Â 
Table Manners of the Avant-Garde
W. H. Auden and Christopher Isherwood went to China during the Sino-Japanese War in 1938. 
This is a not untypical dispatch from them in ''Journey to a War'' (Paragon House).
We kept swapping specially dainty morsels with our neighbours. 
Auden and I developed a private game: it was a point of honour to praise most warmly the dishes you liked least. 
''Delicious,'' Auden murmured, as he munched what was, apparently, a small sponge soaked in glue. 
I replied by devouring, with smiles of exquisite pleasure, an orange which tasted of bitter aloes and contained, in its centre, a large weevil. 
On the whole the food was very nice, but our hosts disparaged it out of courtesy - and of course we had to protest: ''Horrible stuff, this. 
We must apologize. 
. . .''
''No, no!
Not horrible. 
Wonderful!''
''Very poor after your English cookery.''
''English cookery disgusting!
Chinese cookery marvellous!''
Â 
The Poem as a Put-Up Job
Students have every right to distrust a teacher who reads them his own poems. 
This is from ''Memories and Hallucinations: A Memoir'' by D. M. Thomas (Penguin).
I am frightened by the coincidences that seem to cluster around art - even bad art or non-art. 
Once, I was reading to a class of students a poem I'd written about a nestling. 
Our cat, grey Lucina, had mauled the baby bird before we could interfere. 
The poem was new, I thought it better than it was; it would later go into the wastepaper basket. 
As I was reading the weak verses to my class, my voice full of compassion and vanity, there was a knock on the classroom door. 
One of my colleagues entered, his hands cupped around something tiny. 
''I found this outside,'' he explained, in a troubled voice; ''can anyone suggest what I can do with it?''
My students gasped; he was showing us an injured nestling.
The students thought it was a put-up job. 
As though we'd have conspired to maim a nestling in order to amaze them.
Â 
Heaven Hangs On
Though contemporary life lends itself more easily to ideas of hell, a surprising number of Americans still believe in heaven. 
This is from ''Heaven: A History'' by Colleen McDannell and Bernhard Lang (Vintage).
In a Gallup Poll published in 1982, 71 per cent of the American public answered ''yes'' to the question: Do you think there is a heaven where people who have led good lives are eternally rewarded?
This figure was only one per cent less than in 1952, and showed a small increase since 1965. 
Those who believed in heaven outnumbered those who believed in reincarnation by more than three to one. 
When the pollsters, however, tried to ascertain what one actually does in heaven, the polls revealed that the images of the modern heaven, in existence since the eighteenth century, had greatly faded. 
While 54 per cent of those polled assumed that they would be in the presence of God or Jesus Christ in heaven or an afterlife, only 19 per cent believed that people would have responsibilities there. 
Less than half assumed that they would see their friends, relatives, or spouses. 
Although one third believed they would grow spiritually, only 18 per cent thought that they would grow intellectually. 
. . . Only 5 per cent of those polled thought that eternity would be boring.

ï»¿
ARABIC IS A RICH language. 
There are words for losing one's children, for a carriage taking a virgin into battle, for a disease striking camels in the head. 
But when I was sweltering in Cairo in the early 1980's, while studying Arabic, what struck me most was that there was only one word, talg, that refers, if somewhat hazily, to either ice or snow.
At the time I was yearning for a good talg-fall in Cairo, I learned that the Eskimo language has several dozen words for "snow."
Which makes perfect sense: the diversity in a language reflects the interests and obsessions of the society speaking it. 
As a continuing student of the Chinese language, I find that Chinese is especially rich in the specific areas one would expect, given the culture.
There are at least 19 words for silk, for example, and 8 for rice. 
Why?
Well, gao refers to a tough, white silk; qi is a patterned silk; qian is a blue-red silk fabric; kuang is uncombed silk thread; si is regular silk thread; chou is another term for silk fabrics, and so on. 
As for rice, fan refers to the cooked product; dao to the rice when it is still in the paddy; xian to long-grained rice; mi to the husked kernels, and, in some dialects, gu means unhusked kernels.
Since the Chinese care even more for their families than they do for their rice or silk, there is a profusion of words for relations. 
For instance, Chinese has five words for "uncle."
It depends on whether he is your father's older or younger brother, or your mother's brother, or your father's sister's husband, or your mother's sister's husband. 
In English, the word "cousin" is applied to males as well as females, older people as well as younger people, maternal as well as paternal relations. 
Not so in Chinese; the rules that apply to "uncle" also apply to "cousin."
When Americans hurl abuse at each other, they sometimes question each other's paternity or bring in each other's mothers. 
But the Chinese denounce uncles and grandfathers as well as parents, and one common insult calumniates the preceding 18 generations of the accursed one's family.
Chinese has about two dozen expressions for "wife," but in this case the richness of the language doesn't indicate any special esteem. 
On the contrary, most of the terms are unflattering: "the inside person," "the old woman," "the one on the bed," "the children's mother," "the cook."
One reason for the many expressions may be that until early this century it wasn't unusual for peasant women not to have given names. 
As they grew up, they were identified by numbers: second sister, fourth sister and so on.
"My mother didn't have a name, as far as I know," says an octogenarian friend who grew up in the countryside. 
I asked him what his father called his mother, and his brow furrowed. 
Then his face lighted up. 
" 'Hey,' " he said triumphantly. 
"He called her 'Hey.'
"
Where English is particularly rich, and Chinese poor, is in the areas of science and democracy -- the two slogans that since 1919 have been a rallying cry for change. 
Indeed, "science" and "democracy" are sometimes known as S Xiansheng (Mr. S) and D Xiansheng (Mr. D), to signify that they are foreign guests who still have not taken up Chinese residency.
Although law, fa, is an ancient concept in China, it historically wasn't a champion of individual rights but a means of punishment. 
Indeed, the only area of the law in which the Chinese language distinguishes itself is in the designation of punishments. 
Gua refers to execution by slicing (a convict literally cut into pieces); yi refers to the cutting off of a felon's nose. 
(Both are mercifully no longer judicial sentences.)
Most of China's political vocabulary is relatively recent. 
Chinese expressions for "freedom," "politics," "democracy" and "economy" are all only about a century old. 
And words like "individualism" or "privacy" still have a negative connotation in Chinese, reflecting the traditional lack of concern for individual rights.
"This is a factional language, based on groups rather than individuals, and an inclusive language," says Geremie Barme, an Australian scholar whose mastery of the Chinese language gives other foreigners the "red eye disease" (one of the many expressions for "jealousy").
What's an inclusive language?
In English, we tend to hold each other verbally at arm's length; it's the opposite in Chinese. 
Friends address each other as "Big Brother" or "Big Sister," as a sign of respect, and children are required to address adults who are friends or acquaintances of the family as "Auntie" or "Uncle."
This has to be done carefully, however. 
I once disconcerted a Chinese friend by calling her "Little Sister" -- often a prelude to a pickup.
The two ways of saying "we" in Chinese help explain the usefulness of an inclusive expression. 
The first kind, women (pronounced waugh-mun), refers to the speaker and one or more other people but doesn't include the person being addressed. 
The second kind, zamen, includes the person being addressed. 
Thus, a young woman going out with her boyfriend might tell her parents that "women are leaving," but a group of boys flirting with some girls will suggest that "zamen go to a movie."
By comparison, English looks rather aloof and threadbare for lacking an inclusive "we."
But never mind. 
Za men have another area, besides science and democracy, where English triumphs: sex.
English seems to have far more words that are sex-related than contemporary Chinese. 
(Ancient Chinese pornography is another matter, but that rich vocabulary has been largely forgotten.) No one knows if this is because Americans are obsessed with sex or because the Chinese take lots of cold showers -- hot-water heaters still being a rarity in China. 
A researcher of sexuality in Shanghai is stumped by the linguistic challenge of polling Chinese about their sexual practices. 
There are no common expressions for "foreplay" or "orgasm," and so surveys must resort to vaguer terms that people will at least understand. 
Instead of inquiring about the frequency of "a sexual high tide" -- the technical term for "climax" -- the surveys simply ask women how often they enjoy "a pleasant feeling."
It would be rash to draw conclusions on what this says about the Chinese, especially when there are more than 1.1 billion of them. 
Still, it's nice to know that English has the edge in a few areas. 
Science. Democracy. 
Sex. A language could do worse.

file: On the Trail Of a _Wildman,_ And Creatures Nearly as Elusive.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN the wilderness of Shennonjia Forest in central China investigators are seeking an elusive creature that might be an unknown hominid or the product of farmers' imaginations. 
Whatever it is, the ''wildman'' of China has given members of the International Society of Cryptozoology new food for thought.
Since ancient times, legends have proliferated about unicorns, mermaids, dragons and countless other imaginary creatures, and the search for the Loch Ness monster and the yeti in the Himalayas will probably go on forever. 
The International Society of Cryptozoology does not dismiss the existence of such creatures out of hand, but the group is led by scientists who demand hard evidence supporting any claimed discovery of an unknown beast.
While the chances of finding any of the outlandish monsters that figure in popular myth are remote, members say, there are almost certainly some unknown animals left to discover, perhaps including the wildman.
Over the years, there have been hundreds of reports from farmers about a manlike primate that supposedly stands six feet tall, has human features and knows how to weave bamboo. 
In Hubei and nearby provinces, the ''ye ren'' - Chinese for ''wildman'' - has inspired a legend as pervasive as that of the yeti in the Himalayas and the sasquatch of North America.
Two Americans, Dr. Frank E. Poirier, a professor of anthropology at Ohio State University, and J. Richard Greenwell, secretary of the International Society of Cryptozoology, recently returned from China, where they were shown some hints that the wildman might be real. 
Not entirely persuaded, they did say the evidence was provocative.
The main evidence, Dr. Poirier said in an interview, is a series of analyses conducted by Chinese laboratories of a dozen hairs purportedly left by wildmen in bushes, trees and on the ground. 
Chinese biologists at Huadong University in Shanghai told Dr. Poirier and Mr. Greenwell that a scanning electron microscope had revealed the hairs' microstructure, the interior fibers and surface scales, to be characteristic of primates in general, but not of any known primate species.
A chemical analysis of the hairs was conducted by Dr. Zeng Xianzhaw using a particle accelerator at Fudan University in Shanghai, Dr. Poirier said. 
The analysis, using the photon-induced X-ray emission method, found a ratio of iron to zinc in the hairs characteristic of primates but higher than that of all known primates, including human beings. 
''The Chinese scientists told us that zinc-iron ratios in the hair of primates are highly indicative of species,'' Dr. Poirier said.
Most biologists reject the possibility that ape-men or hominids other than human beings still exist, and Mr. Greenwell acknowledges that the Chinese hairs are unlikely to persuade many doubters.
In 1984, two years after the International Society of Cryptozoology was founded by the French zoologist Bernard Heuvelmans, George Gaylord Simpson denounced cryptozoologists in general and searchers after yetis in particular. 
Dr. Simpson, now deceased, who led many expeditions himself and was regarded as the dean of American paleontologists, wrote that ''humans are the most inventive, deceptive and gullible of all animals. 
Only those characteristics can explain the belief of some humans in creationism, in the arrival of U.F.O.'s or in some aspects of cryptozoology,'' which is ''not a science in the acceptable usage of the term.''
Dr. Poirier himself dismisses most of the previous evidence brought forward by the Chinese authorities to support claims that wildmen exist. 
''Casts of footprints are often produced, but they are worthless for a variety of reasons,'' he said. 
''Feces purporting to come from wildmen have been collected, but they could have come from many common animals.''
Â 
'Exciting and Unexpected News'
But sightings of wildmen in China have been recorded for some 2,500 years, he said, and images of the ye ren appear on many paintings and even ancient currency. 
''This doesn't mean that wildmen exist, but I must say, I am somewhat less skeptical than I was before going to China,'' Dr. Poirier said. 
''I still doubt the existence of those other famous creatures, the yeti, sasquatch and bigfoot.''
The new hair analyses, he said, were the main factor in his change of opinion. 
''This is most exciting and unexpected news,'' he said. 
''For the very first time there is scientific evidence for the possible existence of an unknown primate.''
An analysis of the DNA in the hairs might be helpful, Dr. Poirier said, and Chinese scientists have said one is planned. 
But nothing short of an actual body or a live specimen of the creature would persuade most biologists, he said.
Mr. Greenwell of the cryptozoology society agreed and said that even the hair analysis may be of dubious value. 
''We have to remember that analyses of samples have often turned out to be erroneous, and one shouldn't attach too much significance to them,'' he said.
Â 
Species Thought to Be Extinct
Chances are much better for finding animals already known to science that are generally believed to have become extinct or to have disappeared from certain habitats, Mr. Greenwell said.
The Tucson-based International Society of Cryptozoology is particularly interested at present in reported sightings of thylacines, or ''Tasmanian tigers,'' in western and southeastern Australia. 
The thylacine, a marsupial carnivore, is believed to have died out in mainland Australia several thousand years ago, but thylacines survived until modern times in nearby Tasmania. 
The species is believed to have become extinct with the death of the last thylacine at the zoo in Hobart, Tasmania, in 1936.
''Mainstream biologists deny the possibility that thylacines might have survived in mainland Australia,'' Mr. Greenwell said, ''but they've been proved wrong on other suppositions.''
Among the many zoological surprises of the past century was the discovery of living coelacanths off the coast of Africa in 1938. 
The coelacanth, a large, primitive fish, had previously been believed to have been extinct for many millions of years. 
The logotype symbol of the Society of Cryptozoology, Mr. Greenwell said, is the okapi, a giraffe-like animal previously known only from fossils that was discovered living in the Congo jungle in 1901.
Â 
Looking for the Less Spectacular
The society welcomes the exchange of information on elusive species and is reachable by writing P.O. 
Box 43070, Tucson, Ariz., 85733.
Cryptozoologists are better known, however, for their interest in such elusive or fanciful creatures as the Loch Ness monster and the ''mokele-mbembe,'' a dinosaur supposed by some to be living in remote swampland in central Africa.
''The news media focus on our investigations of reputed monsters,'' Mr. Greenwell said, ''but we're also interested in the scientific search for less spectacular animals. 
The kouprey, a large wild ox, was originally discovered in Cambodia in 1937, and it was rediscovered in 1981 after many experts considered it extinct. 
That was exciting for us. 
We do what we can to help scientists look for such rarities and, if possible, keep them from dying out altogether.''

file: SHOPPER_S WORLD_In Hong Kong, Antique Silks Evoke a Patrician Past.txt
text:
ï»¿
ANTIQUE Chinese textiles are enjoying a great new popularity. 
One reason is that even casual shoppers quickly become intrigued with these highly personal bits of history -- imagining the aristocratic Chinese woman who slipped her bound foot into a tiny pair of four-inch silk shoes, or picturing the pampered Chinese boy who wore embroidered silk earmuffs, each one sliding over an ear like a glove on a hand.
In Hong Kong, shoppers can choose from a fascinating array of antique textiles, from a pair of child's earmuffs for $30 (prices are in United States currency at 7.8 Hong Kong dollars to one United States dollar) to an embroidered rank badge worn by a Mandarin official that sells for $150 to a magnificent dragon robe costing $12,000.
"I think in the United States you are more likely to see either very costly robes, or little bits of embroidery that are pretty and inexpensive but have no historical importance," said an art expert in Hong Kong who does not sell textiles but follows the market. 
"Here, dealers have a wider range of items for sale, and they pay more attention to the history of the pieces."
Valery M. Garrett, a Hong Kong collector and a lecturer and writer on Chinese textiles, said that while they are sold in New York, London, Taiwan and occasionally Singapore, Hong Kong has the greatest concentration of these pieces.
Generally, items will be less expensive in Hong Kong because there is no sales tax and, because they are antiques, no duty is charged when the textiles are brought back to the United States. 
Most of the pieces for sale date from the Ming (1368-1644) or Ching dynasties (1644-1912), although some earlier pieces are available.
These textiles are interesting works of art that are highly decorative. 
The colorful Chinese robes look striking when mounted inside a large plexiglass frame. 
The antique earmuffs, collars, sleeve bands and other pieces also make handsome decorations, matted in silk and framed, or framed in plexiglass.
Dealers say the rank badges, one of the newly popular collector's items, are sought after because they have an interesting history, are relatively inexpensive (prices begin under $200) and look very handsome when framed. 
"These badges were worn by imperial officials and by the military during earlier dynasties, but the wearing of the badges was really formalized during the Ching dynasty," said Ms. Garrett, who has written a book on the badges, "Mandarin Squares: Mandarins and Their Regalia," published by Oxford University Press.
The nine civil service rank badges for officials used different birds to symbolize ranks, while the military badges featured beasts such as dragons or lions. 
Ms. Garrett said that by the mid-19th century, wealthy merchants began to buy ranks, the way some Westerners purchased European titles.
"You could also buy a rank for an ancestor, so a merchant might buy a high civil service rank for his grandfather, who was really an illiterate farmer," Ms. Garrett said. 
"Then he would commission a portrait that would show the relative in fine robes decorated with his important rank badge."
Though Hong Kong borders on China and the mainland is easily accessible, buyers here say few antique fabric pieces are coming out of China now. 
The damp climate and even the politics of the mainland -- all kinds of antiquities were destroyed during the Cultural Revolution there in the late 1960's -- work against their preservation.
In fact, Ms. Garrett said, "Generally, it has been the Westerners, the foreigners in China, who revered these pieces and collected them."
Today, there are many sources outside the mainland, from sons and daughters of Chinese families who left China to the relatives of missionaries, merchants and other colonial officials who once lived and worked there.
While a number of stores now carry some kind of antique textiles, three highly regarded shops here are particularly worth visiting because their salespeople are adept at explaining the history of the pieces they offer and the symbolism of the designs.
Taken together, the shops offer a good indication of what Hong Kong has to offer. 
At Teresa Coleman Fine Arts, a small, bright gallery on hilly Wyndham Street in central Hong Kong, the long, narrow wooden drawers hold all kinds of treasures: embroidered fan cases (long, thin triangles of silk), delicate women's shoes and small purses, sleeve bands that once encircled the wide sleeves of Chinese robes, rank badges, earmuffs, robes and shawls. 
This shop offers the greatest array of antique textiles in Hong Kong and is a perfect place to visit for an introduction to the market.
A tiny pair of deep pink silk shoes here, dating from about 1870 and made for a woman with bound feet, is barely four inches long. 
Foot binding began as a court custom and as tiny feet became the vogue and were deemed beautiful and erotic, the painful practice eventually spread to all but the poorest classes in China, becoming popular toward the end of the 11th century and continuing into the 1930's. 
Little girls would have their toes broken, bent back and tightly bound between the ages of three and five, so that the foot developed as a small stump.
Belinda Winard, a salesperson at Teresea Coleman, said three and a half inches was considered the ideal length of a bound foot, though that was not always achieved. 
These pink shoes, which sell for $282, are embroidered with blue lotus flowers with a ribbon border of red and gold.
A lovely cream-colored silk collar from the 19th century with a black ribbon border, made to wear with a woman's robe, has four distinct gourd-shaped sections, each embroidered with a garden scene depicting one of the four seasons. 
The collar is priced at $256.
A pair of military rank badges worn by a fifth-rank officer, worked in petit point, with the beast, a bear, appliqued on top, sells for $614. 
The badges, which are the usual size of 12 by 12 inches, have a sky blue background; the bear is done in yellows, greens and reds, his eyes facing a bold red sun. 
The bear stands on the waters and waves pattern, surround by swastikas, ancient symbols for infinite good luck.
The large, airy Plum Blossoms gallery in central Hong Kong's glittering Exchange Square carries a smaller, more expensive collection of Chinese textiles. 
Stephen McGuinness, the managing director, has sold to private collectors and to museums around the world, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. 
Currently, one of his prized pieces is a 10th-century tapestry fragment priced at $120,000. 
The tapestry features prancing lions woven in greens, purples, reds and blues on a black background. 
The rectangular piece of cloth is thought to have come from a robe, he said. 
This piece came from a monastery in Tibet, a country that has recently become an important source of rare old textiles.
"THE monasteries in Tibet were virtual treasure troves, and they are the source for most of the pieces coming from China today," Mr. McGuinness said. 
"Tibet is high and dry and its climate helped preserve textile pieces. 
Its monasteries, which had Chinese wall hangings, silk curtains and robes, had thick stone walls that kept the articles at constant, cool temperatures."
Moreover, he said, the monasteries were repositories for Chinese clothing, because the style-conscious aristocracy donated what were considered unstylish clothes.
A later, less expensive piece is a curtain panel that dates from about 1760. 
It is 10 feet of midnight blue silk and gold brocade, the gold design featuring pairs of dragons chasing a pearl, which was the wish-granting gem of the Chinese. 
That piece is priced at $7,000.
A late-19th-century Chinese tablecloth studded with little round mirrors is embroidered with the Hundred Antiques motif, which includes bronze vases and platters. 
It sells for $800.
"This altar cloth was the kind of thing usually presented to wealthy Chinese at their 60th or 70th birthday party," Mr. McGuinness said. 
"It symbolizes their wealth, their importance."
At Charlotte Horstmann & Gerald Godfrey, one of Asia's most respected antique galleries, there are baskets full of small Chinese purses, earmuffs and sleeve bands in the shop at Ocean Terminal Center on the Kowloon side of the harbor. 
A six-inch royal blue silk purse from the 19th century, with a lovely garden scene, sells for only $19. 
The tiny stitches, each as small as a pinpoint, are known as blind stitches because the close work involved was said to inevitably lead to blindness in the seamstress. 
Hiroko Wilde, a salesperson, explained that for this reason, very young people sewed this stitch because by middle age their eyes failed. 
The work was also known as forbidden stitches because until the late 19th century they were reserved for members of the court.
A pair of cream-colored sleeve bands are decorated with geese, butterflies and peonies in beige, browns and blues, all embroidered in the blind stitch. 
They are mounted in plexiglass frames and priced at $1,126. 
Horstmann's also has what it calls a warehouse of antiques downstairs from the shop, where serious collectors can look at more robes and tapestries.
"Chinese gowns were once regarded as decorative objects to be worn, cut up or remade in another style, but today people have a new respect, a new awareness of their beauty and worth," said Gerald Godfrey.
In a recent visit, the warehouse had a beautiful 19th-century gown in a rich yellow-gold silk. 
Made in China for a Tibetan monk, it was lined in soft sea otter fur. 
The silk woven covered in small stylized bats, which symbolize happiness to the Chinese. 
The robe sells for $7,400.
Â 
BUYING SILKS
All three shops are closed on Sunday.
Teresa Coleman Fine Arts, 37 Wyndham Street, Ground Floor, Central, Hong Kong; telephone 526 2450. 
Open 9:30 A.M. to 6 P.M.
Plum Blossoms, Room 305-307 in Tower One, Exchange Square, 8 Connaught Place, Hong Kong; 521 2189. 
Open 10 A.M. to 6:30 P.M.

file: Spectacular Fossils Record Early Riot of Creation.txt
text:
ï»¿
NEW fossil discoveries in China, hailed as among the most spectacular in this century, show that the dramatic transformation of life from primeval single-cell organisms to the complex multicellular precursors of modern fauna was more sudden, swift and widespread than scientists had thought.
From cream-colored sediments of what was a sea floor 570 million years ago, paleontologists have extracted specimens of 70 species of trilobites, worms, sponges and various ancestors of crustaceans, spiders and insects. 
They are not only the oldest such fossils ever found but, more remarkably, their soft-body parts as well as skeletal and shell remains are unusually well-preserved.
The fossils give scientists their first glimpse of the strange creatures that populated the seas in the early stage of what is known as the Cambrian explosion. 
The Cambrian geological period, from 570 million to 500 million years ago, saw the appearance of increasingly complex marine animals in a riot of shapes and anatomical designs anticipating much of life as it is today.
Scientists are not sure what touched off this riotous proliferation of more advanced life forms after three billion years in which life never rose above the rudimentary level of bacteria, algae and some primitive worms. 
Life did not begin appearing on land until after the Cambrian period.
Dr. Jan Bergstrom, a paleontologist at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm who analyzed the Chinese fossils, said they suggested that the Cambrian transition was "a revolution perhaps more than evolution."
Most of the Chinese fossils, Dr. Bergstrom said, resemble species identified in the Burgess Shale, the 530-million-year-old fossil beds in the Canadian Rockies that have been the main source of knowledge of that crucial period.
The similarities are the basis for the conclusion that the diversification and proliferation of new life forms must have occurred rapidly at the outset of the Cambrian period.
"Evolution of these creatures seems to have been a sudden and widespread phenomenon," Dr. Bergstrom and colleagues wrote in the current issue of Research and Exploration, a scholarly journal of the National Geographic Society.
The Chinese fossils were discovered in 1984 at Chengjiang, in the southern province of Yunnan, by Dr. Hou Xianguang of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology. 
Dr. Chen Junyuan, also of the institute, is continuing excavations at the site.
But the first descriptions of the fossils were largely confined to Chinese publications and received little attention from scientists elsewhere. 
This is changing, though, with the new analysis led by Dr. Bergstrom, an authority on trilobites, ubiquitous creatures of that period that have long been extinct. 
His collaborators include Maurits Lindstrom, a geologist at Stockholm University, and Dr. Chen and Dr. Hou.
As the full import of the discovery is recognized, scientists are describing the fossils as "genesis material" and one of the most exciting finds since the ancient marine life in the Burgess Shale was first explored in 1909. 
"All eyes are on Stockholm," said Gregory D. Edgecombe, a paleontologist at the American Museum of Natural History in New York. 
He said the preservation of the Chinese fossils was even better than in the Burgess material.
Dr. Andrew Knoll, a Harvard University expert on early life, said: "We knew from the Burgess that there was a tremendous diversity of life in the Cambrian. 
Most of everything that was going to happen, all the ways of making invertebrate animals, had already happened by the mid-Cambrian. 
Now, it seems the new life forms were invented within the first few million years of the Cambrian."
A few million years is but a blink of the eye in the geological and evolutionary time scale. 
And Dr. Bergstrom said it was quite possible that at this time "you could have the formation of an entirely new type of animal within thousands of years."
Calling the Chinese fossils "fascinating and important," Dr. Steven M. Stanley, a paleontologist at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland and author of "The New Evolutionary Timetable," said he was not surprised that they resembled the Burgess specimens. 
"We've known there had to be rapid diversification of life at that time," he said.
Â 
Unusually Well Preserved
The Chengjiang fauna lived on the sea bottom or just below or above it, along a broad continental shelf beneath fairly shallow waters. 
Even some of the animals without hard skeletons or shells were preserved intact, which is extremely rare. 
Skeletonized animals make up more than 99 percent of the fossil record.
Dr. Bergstrom could only speculate on the conditions leading to such deposits of ancient invertebrate life.
"A violent storm probably stirred up the sea bottom and the mud settled over a large area, cutting off the animals' oxygen and preserving them," he said. 
"You can go 30 miles in one direction and 12 in another and still come up with fossils."
Despite their great age, a majority of the fossil species at Chengjiang belong to animal groups that still exist, including sponges, certain worms, bivalves of the brachiopod group and arthropods. 
Indeed, arthropods dominate the fossil bed with at least 30 species. 
These include three species of trilobites and several creatures with long tails that looked like shrimp. 
The arthropods' descendants are crustaceans, insects and spiders, and the family resemblances can be seen that far back.
For example, the Alalcomenaeus, also found in the Burgess Shale, has distinctive large appendages on its head. 
Similarly, Jianfengia looks like a small shrimp, and though it lacks typical antennas, it does have "great appendages" on the head.
The second most common group consists of sponges, most of which bear a striking similarity to the Burgess Shale sponge fauna. 
Other creatures were distantly related to the jellyfish, some flat and others shaped like a corkscrew or spindle. 
The tallest stood almost two feet above the sea floor. 
One carried a large disk with concentric air chambers divided into numerous partitions.
Dr. Bergstrom's team is not sure what to make of some of the specimens. 
The largest animal found, a two-foot-long predator, had stout, segmented arms and a round mouth encircled with cutting "knives."
One puzzle is whether this is a type of worm or an arthropod.
Other fascinating specimens include worms with a proboscis armed with spines and a long creature that looks like a worm with a shelly hat.
Â 
Worm With 'Kneecaps'
"The real shocker for me is the worm that looks like it has kneecaps," said Dr. Ellis L. Yochelson, a paleontologist at the Smithsonian Institution. 
He was referring to an animal known as Microdictyon.
In earlier discoveries, scientists had noticed the tiny shell-like plates that Dr. Yochelson likened to kneecaps. 
But they had no way of knowing or suspecting that the plates would sit on a wormlike animal.
In their report, Dr. Bergstrom and his colleagues said these plates were situated in 10 pairs along the body of the Microdictyon. 
From the area of each pair of plates extended a pair of very long legs or tentacles. 
"The body design," they said, "seems completely unlikely, but it must once have been functional."
Dr. Yochelson said: "The record of extremely complicated organisms has been pushed back significantly by this find. 
And it says there was a much shorter interval than expected for the evolution of multicellular animals with hard parts."

text:
ï»¿
Miles and miles from nowhere, carved into a cliff here in the arid desolation of northwestern China, are 492 caves lined with some of the finest Buddhist art in the world.
For up to 1,600 years, the dry desert air has preserved the vivid painted murals that fill the cave interiors, along with hundreds of painted statues ranging from life-size to 108 feet tall.
These days, however, the caves face a new threat: enthusiastic visitors. 
Some 150,000 people visited the grottoes in 1988 - nearly as many as in the entire four decades since the Communist revolution. 
The overwhelming majority of visitors are from other parts of China, but the number of foreigners is also soaring: from just 462 in 1979, when the Government opened the area to foreigners, to 30,000 in 1988.
''It's a wonderful thing and it's a terrible thing,'' said Duan Wenjie, the 72-year-old director of the Dunhuang Research Institute, who has lived here 44 years. 
''If people come in large numbers, then they risk hurting the treasures they have come to see.''
So Mr. Duan and his colleagues have agreed to a painful solution: they will build eight cave replicas and sharply curtail access to the originals. 
As it is now, only 30 of the caves are open to the public; after the mock-ups are completed by 1993, only a few of the originals will remain open. 
All the others will be padlocked to protect them.
Â 
A Familiar Dilemma
The same dilemma is faced by curators all over the world: how to allow people to enjoy artistic treasures without harming them. 
The compromises vary: putting glass over fine Rembrandts; installing a plexiglass shield in front of Michelangelo's ''Pieta'' and roping off the area in front of outstanding works.
The paleolithic caves at Lascaux, France, were closed after deterioration to the outstanding paintings there. 
And admittance to the paleolithic paintings in the Altamira Caves in Spain is restricted, although a simulation of the caves has been opened to the public in Madrid.
''Our method solves the dilemma of protecting the caves, while still allowing people to appreciate them,'' asserted Fan Jinshi, the deputy director of the Dunhuang institute. 
''The eight copies are representatives of the very best caves. 
You can't say that visitors will see less.''
The Dunhuang caves, also known as the Mogaoku Grottoes, were painstakingly carved into a cliff a mile long. 
The first caves were dug in A.D. 366, and the finest examples probably date from the Tang Dynasty, a golden age in China lasting from 618 to 907. 
In most cases the entire interior is brightly painted: portraits, geometric designs and murals depicting famous Buddhist scenes. 
The murals cover an area equivalent to more than one and a half football fields, and the caves also house some 2,000 painted sculptures.
Â 
'Discovered' in 1900
The artwork was paid for by wealthy Buddhists and by the imperial court, for in those days Dunhuang was a stopping point along the silk route, and a far more important city than it is today. 
But as the silk route faded, so did Dunhuang. 
The last caves here were carved during the Ming Dynasty, which lasted from 1368 to 1644.
Local monks guarded the caves continually, but the treasury was only ''discovered'' by the world in 1900, after a Taoist monk accidentally found a sealed-off cave containing 40,000 to 50,000 documents from eight dynasties. 
Foreigners made their way to the area and carried away not only the priceless manuscripts but also some outstanding examples of sculptures and murals that are now in Britain, France, India and the Soviet Union.
After the Communists took over in 1949, Prime Minister Zhou Enlai became a great patron of Dunhuang. 
He authorized money to buttress the cliff face with cement and install locked doors on all the caves, changing the site's appearance but also protecting it from erosion and earthquakes.
The opening to foreign tourists led to the construction of a small airport nearby and to growing numbers of visitors, both domestic and foreign. 
The overseas tourists, 60 percent of whom are Japanese, are particularly valued because of the money they spend. 
They have been a tremendous boon to the local economy - per capita income is about $100 a year -but unfortunately, the tourists breathe. 
The moist carbon dioxide they exhale is thought to be unsettling to murals that for centuries have been accustomed to desert air.
Â 
Long Trip for the Reward
A crucial question, of course, is whether foreigners will be willing to travel so far - 1,150 miles west of Beijing, approximately as far from the capital as Omaha is from New York - to see mostly reproductions, and a small but so far undetermined number of real caves. 
Local officials, who have relatively little experience with overseas tourists, are optimistic; indeed, they seem surprised even at the question.
They emphasize that conditions in the copied caves will be much better than in the real ones: not only will these be among the best examples of the artistic treasures at Dunhuang, but lighting will be better and there will be special audio-visual presentations to explain the history of the caves. 
The mock-up caves will be in an exhibition hall facing the cliff.
''There won't be much impact on tourism,'' said Ying Guangling, an official of the local tourism bureau in the modern town of Dunhuang, whose 10,000 residents live 25 miles across the desert from the caves. 
''Visitors will still see some of the real caves, so they'll be satisfied.''

text:

As his two children run about his small apartment, dodging his easel and smearing their fingers across his palette, Song Bin paints ''Mona Lisas'' - more than 100 of them so far.
Nearby, in a studio about as big as a queen-size bed, two Chinese artists have been painting European masterpieces by the hundreds. 
Like many other artists who fled from China to Hong Kong, they have given up hope of painting masterpieces of their own and earn money by reproducing the works of others. 
It has become a local cottage industry - copying the tranquil countrysides of Winslow Homer, the Tahitian beauties of Paul Gauguin and the famous works of other well-known painters, to the dot, stroke and hue.
Each year this city, tapping a cheap army of talented artists from the territory of Hong Kong or the neighboring Chinese province of Guangdong, exports thousands of copies of European masterpieces to Europeans and Americans, who choose what they want in mail-order catalogues. 
Patterns and samples are toted across the border to Shenzhen or Canton, and the painted replicas are carried back.
Usually, the artistic result is an adequate replica. 
Buyers know they are not getting the real thing, and the paintings would not fool experts, but the replicas cost a tiny fraction of what the original would bring. 
And if an exact copy seems too kitschy, the buyer can ask the artist to add a tree or a road to tailor the scene to the local environment or even the living-room furniture.
''Americans like the Renoirs, van Goghs and Manets, and they like big paintings,'' said Daniel Chui, the owner of Ultra Art, a Hong Kong company that deals in commercial art. 
''In England, they like Constables or Turners. 
In Germany, they like small portraits and dark paintings of animals and still lifes of flowers.''
A few years ago ''Mona Lisas'' were extremely popular, but the demand seems to have subsided. 
Since last year demand for the great masters has been declining, restricted mainly to buyers in Europe. 
Meanwhile, interest in commercial art - anything from a picture of a puppy to a swirl of lines and dots - has risen, particularly among Americans.
This trend can prove disappointing for the young Chinese artists who may want to paint ''Mona Lisas''; if the buyers want California landscapes, the copyists' study of the old masters suffers. 
Xu Zhicheng, a 28-year-old artist who escaped from China to Hong Kong a decade ago, has been painting more replicas of American landscapes and seascapes than of Turner seascapes.
Copying masterpieces over and over may seem less peculiar to a Chinese artist than to a Westerner. 
It is what Chinese painters have historically done, painting tree after tree and waterfall after waterfall to develop an artistic style. 
On the other hand, artists trained solely in traditional Chinese methods and esthetics might find it difficult not only to adapt to oil paints and Western brushes, but also to understand the enthusiasm of European artists for biblical scenes, fruit, Gothic churches and even nudes. 
Still, they tend to adapt quickly.
''When you look at a masterpiece for the first time, you won't know how to paint it,'' said You Zhong-Ping, who shares the cramped workshop with Mr. Xu. But painting a piece the second time around is much easier, Mr. Xu chimed in, adding that he often retouches the first copy: ''I don't completely understand their way of thinking or their ideology. 
I just paint until it looks right.''
Song Bin believes that an artist must understand the subject he or she is painting. 
Life in Wenzhou, the eastern Chinese city where he was born, differed fundamentally, of course, from the Western life style. 
He studied traditional Chinese painting and woodcut engraving at the Zhejiang Arts School in eastern China and graduated in 1966, on the eve of the Cultural Revolution, an upheaval that eviscerated the country's artistic expression for a decade. 
He came to Hong Kong in 1978.
Now 45, he still tries to bone up on the mores of the European upper classes and the history of the Renaissance and reads library books on art. 
He asks for the best possible pictures of the paintings he is to produce and scours the galleries of Hong Kong for original oil paintings in order to pick up tips on brush strokes, texture and blends of paint. 
''My training in watercolors didn't help much,'' he said.
Having painted the ''Mona Lisa'' so often, Mr. Song said he has learned how to apply the subtle touches of color for her face: a light layer of red, then a bit of yellow highlight and then a thin layer of white, which brings out a slight glow in her cheeks.
The corners of her mouth, he said, are still the hardest to portray because her smile has a feminine and maternal quality that is hard to capture. 
''You can't paint her smile too broadly,'' he said. 
''It's got to be delicate and subtle. 
You must understand her status in society, her personality.''
Copy artists are paid by the piece, according to the type of painting and the quality produced. 
Mr. You explained that a medium-size painting might take three to five days and bring about $200. 
Prices also vary according to genre. 
''French Impressionist paintings are cheaper than the Michelangelos,'' said Song Bin, ''even though the Impressionist works are harder to paint.''
Mr. Song, who calls himself a modern realist painter and relies on copying to support his family, earns about $960 a month, producing about 10 copies a week. 
But it takes him at least a week to paint a ''Mona Lisa,'' he said, and longer if the customer wants a good replica. 
He earns about $250 for a ''Mona Lisa,'' which is sold in Europe or America for much more.
The Hong Kong artists have faced stiff competition recently, as companies have gone directly into China to recruit artists for less money. 
An artist there can earn the equivalent of a month's salary in a week by copying.
Moreover, those artists, too, are eager to learn the Western style of painting. 
Only at China's best academies are artists encouraged to express their emotions and feelings, and to develop a personal style in their art. 
Any training in oil painting is generally scanty.
''They learn about light, color and shading as a set of rules,'' said Wang Yang, the director of the Institute of Chinese Painting and Calligraphy at Shenzhen University, ''but actually it should not be thought of in those terms.''
By copying masterpieces, he said, his students are forced to try to understand the thinking and the spirit of the original artist. 
''The original artist interpreted nature in a certain way. 
By copying, the Chinese artist must also delve into his mind and his own personality to re-create the work.''
Mr. Wang said he also tells his students that although they must absorb Western methods, they must be prepared to discard them in order to create a style of their own. 
Nevertheless, many artists who have been copying for a while acknowledge that though they tire of masterpieces they have painted dozens of times, they are drawn to the European tradition. 
After months or years of immersion in bright yellows and oranges, cathedrals and ballet dancers, copy artists turning to their own work find it hard to revive the simple line and form of the Chinese style and to tone down the brilliant colors favored by Western schools.
For Mr. Song, the daily mimesis of a masterpiece reminds him constantly that his work is not an art but a trade. 
Yet he said the Western style is already so much a part of him that he couldn't abandon it and return to traditional Chinese styles. 
Thedeep colors and splashes of light of Western art challenge him more than does Chinese painting, with its reverence for the line.
''Someday,'' he added, ''I'd like to be able to bring together the drawing of the line with the technique of light and shade.''
